point-01.caption: Placement Before Ukeire
point-01.situation: A South-round decision where the hand is not forced yet, but the current order changes the value of every discard. You may be leading with a cushion, chasing a reachable seat, or trying to escape last. The candidate tiles are close enough in efficiency that point thresholds and future danger should decide the tie.
point-01.read: First ask what point change matters, then read the hand. A 1,000-point win that ends a dangerous dealer turn can be excellent from first, while the same win from fourth may be almost meaningless. LuckyJ's top-half games were built on more wins and far fewer deal-ins, so the hand must be judged by both conversion and loss avoidance. The leader low-risk signal in the data is honest but small: copy it only when the safer tile still leaves the hand with a real way forward. If value is required, preserve riichi, dora, and mangan material before the hand narrows. If the lead is the asset, make the next discard easier instead of chasing a decorative upgrade.
point-01.whyNot: Pure efficiency is tempting because it gives a clean answer: keep the most ukeire and let the hand decide later. What it misses is that later may be too late. By iishanten, the hand may already be trapped into a 1,000-point outcome that does not matter, or into a live discard you never needed to face.
point-01.copy: When two discards are close, first name the point change you need: end the hand cheaply, reach 5,200, threaten mangan, or protect the lead. If the cheap line is enough, choose the lower-friction tile. If the cheap line is not enough, keep the tile that makes the hand worth pushing, provided it does not create immediate danger.
point-01.limit: Do not use this to justify killing a clearly superior shape. If one tile gains a strong tenpai or a much better wait and the safer alternative only feels comfortable, take the real hand unless the score table makes defense mandatory.

point-02.caption: Keep the Anchor
point-02.situation: The hand is still early and not yet honest: two-shanten or worse, several candidate blocks, and at least one pair, triplet, dora, red five, or yakuhai that could define the hand later. No opponent has forced a strict fold yet, so the main question is not pure ukeire. You are deciding which pieces still deserve time.
point-02.read: A useful early anchor is not merely a pair. It is the piece that lets the hand become open, valuable, or defensible without needing a perfect sequence of draws. Pair and triplet anchors are especially important because they can turn into yakuhai calls, toitoi pressure, chiitoi fallback, or a stable pair for a normal hand. Dora and red-five material deserve the same respect when they make the final hand worth pushing. The key is that the tile must have a concrete second job; keeping it because it feels important is not enough.
point-02.whyNot: The pure-efficiency discard is tempting because it makes the hand look like a normal five-block riichi hand immediately. What it misses is that many early hands are not yet normal, and forcing them to be normal can erase the best value or open option before you know which draw is coming.
point-02.copy: When the hand is early and messy, first mark the tiles that provide yaku, dora value, call permission, or an emergency stop. If one of those tiles also supports your shape, keep it and cut the weak block that needs the most exact help.
point-02.limit: Do not protect anchors after their job expires. If the hand has a fast good-shape path, or the kept tile is a dead honor, isolated terminal, or pair that cannot become yaku, value, or safety, take the efficient discard.

point-03.caption: Open With a Reason
point-03.situation: You have a clumsy hand with one or two bad blocks, possible yakuhai or tanyao, and an early call opportunity. The offered tile is useful, but taking it will remove riichi, ura, and menzen-tsumo from the hand. The table has not yet forced you to defend, so this is a construction decision, not a panic button.
point-03.read: A call is strongest when it changes what the hand is allowed to do. Ponning yakuhai creates a legal hand; chiing into tenpai changes the clock; calling to deny a dealer draw may be correct even for a small hand. The normal open tanyao or yakuhai hand is often 1,000 to 3,900, so the tempo must be real enough to compensate for losing the closed premium. LuckyJ's record is active but selective: about 36% of hands involved calls, while roughly 2,000 engine-preferred calls were passed. Copy the selectivity, not the surface aggression. If the call only improves shape while leaving no yaku, no tenpai plan, and no safe reserve, it has not earned the exposure.
point-03.whyNot: Pure closed-hand thinking says to pass because riichi, ura, and menzen tsumo are valuable. That is true when the hand can actually reach them. It misses the bad-hand case where two weak blocks make the closed 3,900 a story you tell yourself while opponents win a cheap hand first.
point-03.copy: First check yaku, distance, value, and the next safe tile. If the call creates a legal hand, immediate tenpai, a strong one-shanten, or a specific tempo gain, take it and discard the tile that keeps the hand coherent. If none of those conditions is true, keep the hand closed and let the table give you more information.
point-03.limit: Do not use this to justify opening every bad shape. Good closed value, a live riichi path, all-last point requirements that demand a bigger hand, or an open hand with no defensive exit all argue for passing.

point-04.caption: Open, Keep Brakes
point-04.situation: You have already called, or you are considering a call that will shorten the hand. The hand may be yakuhai, tanyao, honitsu, or a keiten chase, but it is not guaranteed to win immediately. One or more honors, genbutsu, or suji tiles compete with ordinary shape tiles.
point-04.read: Open hands need defensive design because they have fewer tiles left to choose from. A closed hand can sometimes draw into safety while staying flexible; an open hand must often defend with the material it kept before the threat appeared. That is why a 1,000-point open hand still two-shanten should not casually spend its only genbutsu, while a 3,900 tenpai can justify more commitment. A saved genbutsu buys one turn, not a permanent fold. Once it is spent, the next draw decides whether mawashi still exists: a new genbutsu or low-danger discard that preserves one-shanten keeps the hand alive; an improvement to good tenpai can justify a fresh push; if only a live tile preserves the shape, the choice has become an honest push or a fold that breaks the hand. When LuckyJ is fourth against a third-place dealer's riichi, winning gains defensive value because it ends the dealer turn and prevents the gap from widening. Directly dealing into that dealer is also the worst transfer, so the desire to stop them does not authorize a chain of unsafe discards.
point-04.whyNot: Tile efficiency tempts you to cut the safe honor and keep the extra acceptance. That feels clean because the hand is open and therefore supposedly attacking. It misses the future cost: after another call, you may have to choose between folding with no tiles and dealing a live middle tile for a cheap hand. The opposite mistake is treating fourth place as permission to push forever; stopping the dealer matters only while your own winning route is credible enough to compete with the direct deal-in cost.
point-04.copy: Before calling, check distance and the remaining safe tile. After calling, check again: safe to whom, and on which next danger turn? Treat the last genbutsu as a one-turn option. After spending it, start the calculation from zero: continue by mawashi if the new discard is low-friction and preserves the strong one-shanten, push if the draw creates a hand whose value and placement effect pay for the danger, and break the hand when preserving it requires several live tiles. Being fourth against the third-place dealer adds value to winning the hand, but not to merely surviving one risky discard.
point-04.limit: Do not freeze your hand around a stale safe tile, and do not call every no-genbutsu continuation mawashi. Once no tolerable discard preserves the shape, mawashi has ended. If the hand is cheap, the wall is short, or more unsafe discards remain after this one, fold even from fourth; spend safety more freely only when the hand has enough value, immediacy, or placement necessity to justify the whole remaining path.

point-05.caption: Trim Future Danger
point-05.situation: The hand is far from tenpai, usually two-shanten or worse, and contains one or two loose middle tiles outside the main value plan. Opponents may not have declared yet, but rivers are developing and your own earlier discards are starting to make some later releases awkward. The decision is between small present ukeire and a cleaner future push/fold path.
point-05.read: A floater is not harmless just because nobody has riichi yet. If your hand is slow, there is a real chance that danger arrives before your tenpai does. That means an isolated [[4p]], [[5s]], or [[6m]] must be judged by its future release price, not only by how many tiles it accepts today. This idea is strongest when the tile is outside your yaku, outside your dora plan, and not part of the best five blocks. You are not folding early; you are removing the tile that would make a later push irrational.
point-05.whyNot: Pure efficiency wants to keep the central floater because it sees more tiles than a terminal or honor. That is reasonable in a fast hand. In a slow hand, it misses the fact that the hand may have to survive a riichi before those acceptances matter.
point-05.copy: When you are far away, name your value plan first, then identify the leftover tile least connected to it. If that tile is a live middle tile that will be hard to release later, cut it while the table is still cheap.
point-05.limit: Do not turn this into automatic middle-tile hatred. Keep the floater when it is red, dora-connected, the only good-shape upgrade, or required for the score you need.

point-06.caption: Seed Value Early
point-06.situation: An early hand where the fastest version looks cheap, but you still have flexible value material: red fives, dora-adjacent tiles, yakuhai pairs, or pair-heavy structure. The table is not yet forcing defense. The decision is whether to keep a value seed or clean the hand for maximum immediate shape.
point-06.read: Value is easiest to preserve while the hand is wide. If the likely efficient hand is only 1,000 or 2,000 and the hanchan asks for 5,200 or mangan, the efficient line may already be failing. LuckyJ's supported habit here is specific: retain red and dora material that still connects to tanyao, riichi, yakuhai, or a real pair structure. Do not confuse that with buying random risk from behind. A value tile earns its place by making the final hand worth pushing, not by looking expensive in isolation. The moment the value plan stops improving the actual hand, it becomes clutter.
point-06.whyNot: The pure-efficiency cut is tempting because it often increases the hand's immediate cleanliness. It also avoids the embarrassment of holding an honor or dora too long. But if that cleanliness produces a cheap, bad-shape tenpai that you cannot push, the early speed was an illusion.
point-06.copy: When the cheap line is insufficient, keep value material that is connected, pair-based, or naturally callable, and spend terminals or redundant floaters first. Recheck every draw: if the value tile begins to cost real ukeire or real safety, release it. Treat red fives and dora shapes as part of the hand, not as souvenirs.
point-06.limit: Do not apply this to broad risk-taking just because you are behind. Against live threats, or when the value tile is isolated and the hand remains small, choose shape or safety instead.

point-08.caption: Riichi Taxes Everyone
point-08.situation: A closed tenpai or near-tenpai where you can be first to present a real threat. Opponents have not yet shown enough force to make the hand a pure defense problem. The choice is between declaring now, staying dama, or waiting for a prettier upgrade.
point-08.read: Riichi is pressure converted into points. It adds a han, creates uradora upside, and makes every opponent price their next discard under threat. LuckyJ's winning-half games used more riichi, and the sampled pressure riichis receive unusually broad outside-engine support. Mortal usually supports declaring riichi in them, but declaration support does not prove LuckyJ's discard or wait is best. The issue is not reach volume; it is whether the declaration changes the table. Reach when the lock buys value, fold equity, or a necessary placement swing.
point-08.whyNot: The conservative mistake is waiting for the perfect wait after the hand is already strong enough. The reckless mistake is reaching every closed tenpai because riichi is usually good. Both ignore the table: timing, opponent progress, and whether the value actually forces reaction.
point-08.copy: If you are first to credible pressure, your wait is live, and the riichi turns a small hand into a meaningful threat, declare. If the hand is already enough dama, or the riichi merely locks you into future danger, keep the hand quiet. Review not just whether the riichi won, but whether it made opponents change their discards.
point-08.limit: Avoid this against multiple active threats with a low-value bad wait, or in endgame score situations where dama wins the seat you need. Riichi should tax the table, not donate a stick.

point-09.caption: Reprice Every Draw
point-09.situation: You have a playable hand, but the table changes while you are still short of winning: a riichi appears, an open hand adds pressure, or your draw creates a worse next discard. The tempting line is to keep following the plan you chose last turn. This point applies when the hand may need more than one unsafe discard before it can win.
point-09.read: Push-fold is a sequence, not a single-tile quiz. The first discard may be acceptable by itself, but the next draw can turn the continuation into a bad contract. The nondealer Tokujou sample removes every LuckyJ dealer state and every locked discard after LuckyJ's own riichi. It leaves 46 chosen discards at 90% or more on the maximum NAGA danger proxy: all 46 faced at least one riichi, 33 were tenpai, 12 were one-shanten, 20 were open hands, and at least two NAGA heads supported 30. The repeated 99.99% reading behaves like a capped alarm, not a literal deal-in probability. The supported cases are concentrated in valuable tenpai, meaningful riichi declarations, and shortened open hands with very little inventory. The rejected cases show why the alarm still matters.
point-09.whyNot: Pure efficiency wants to preserve ukeire and decides the hand is an attack once. That misses the future-discard bill. It also mistakes tenpai for permission. In the clearest rejected case, LuckyJ protected late open tenpai while leading with 41,000, chose a 99.99% proxy tile over a 2.97% alternative rejected by all three heads, and dealt into a 12,000-point hand. Maintaining tenpai explained the move; it did not justify it.
point-09.copy: First count value and distance, then count the unsafe discards the hand probably still owes. Classify an extreme push before copying it: value-backed tenpai, placement urgency, a pressure riichi, or an inventory trap caused by calls. If the hand is not tenpai or its value is ordinary, choose the line that keeps a safe exit or moves through mawashi instead of paying the whole bill. When a new threat appears, redo the count from zero.
point-09.limit: These counts describe nondealer decisions only; do not mix dealer-continuation value into them. Outcomes were mixed—12 self-wins, 11 direct deal-ins, 14 wins by another player, and nine draws—so a later win does not prove the push was sound. Strong tenpai and All Last score requirements can still demand danger, but the value must be explainable before the result is known.

point-10.caption: Count The Last Row
point-10.situation: The hand has reached the third row with long rivers, at least one live threat, and only a handful of draws left. You may be tenpai, one-away, or barely able to make keiten. Shape language is no longer enough; the decision must be tied to points and safety.
point-10.read: Late decisions are accounting problems. First count the direct win: value, wait quality, and whether the win changes placement. Then count draw tenpai: whether you can reach or keep tenpai through tiles that are genbutsu, suji, kabe-supported, or otherwise low-friction. Finally count the fold: how many safe tiles you have and whether folding now protects the same placement better than a thin push. LuckyJ’s late disagreement rate falling to about 28% is a useful reminder that there is less room for style here. The closer the wall gets to zero, the more every discard must answer an exact point question.
point-10.whyNot: The tempting mistake is to keep using early-hand language: maybe value, maybe shape, maybe one more draw. In the third row, maybe is expensive. A tile that was flexible on turn five may now be only a dangerous discard with no time left to cash its upside.
point-10.copy: With few draws left, write the decision in order: win value, tenpai-payment value, number of safe discards, and next-turn danger. If a discard advances one of those goals without creating a worse next discard, take it; otherwise fold.
point-10.limit: Do not chase keiten through multiple live threats with an unprotected center tile. Also do not overfold a high-value real tenpai just because the row is late; if the hand is worth pushing and the discard is tolerable, attack.

point-11.caption: Keiten Is Value
point-11.situation: A late hand with few tiles left where winning outright has become unlikely, but tenpai is still reachable. One or more opponents may be threatening, and your candidate discards differ mainly in safety and whether they preserve a final tenpai shape. The decision is not attack versus fold, but safe tenpai versus clean noten.
point-11.read: Noten payments are part of the hand's value. A 1,000 to 3,000 swing can protect first, pull you out of last, or force someone else to chase in the next hand. LuckyJ was tenpai in 823 of 1,761 exhaustive draws (46.7%, or 6.3% of all 13,054 hands): this happens often enough that you must study it, not improvise it. The correct keiten chase uses genbutsu, dead tiles, kabe-supported tiles, or tiles already accepted by the threat. The wrong chase asks a dangerous tile to survive just because the wall is short. In late play, count both the payment and the danger of each tile needed to reach it.
point-11.whyNot: Pure defense is tempting because noten feels cheaper than a deal-in, and often it is. Pure attack is tempting because tenpai payments are visible and immediate. Both become wrong when they ignore the exact discard path: safe tenpai is valuable, unsafe keiten is not.
point-11.copy: With the wall short, count how many safe or nearly safe discards get you to tenpai. If the answer is one or two harmless tiles, preserve the shape and take the draw value. If the answer includes a live middle tile against a real threat, fold first and let the payment go.
point-11.limit: Do not apply this when the hand still has a strong winning chance worth pushing normally; then evaluate it as attack. Also do not apply it when tenpai requires danger that exceeds the 1,000 to 3,000 reward.

point-12.caption: Splits Are Homework
point-12.situation: You are reviewing a hand where LuckyJ, Nishiki, the other NAGA heads, or Mortal disagree on the best discard. The move may be early and quiet, or it may be a real push-fold decision with points at stake. The danger is treating one model's answer as a command instead of a question.
point-12.read: The book's method is conditional copying. LuckyJ's top-discard match with NAGA is about 73%, which is high enough to respect the engine and low enough to make the mismatches valuable. Over 36,000 LuckyJ/Nishiki mismatches give plenty of study material, but a mismatch alone does not tell you who is right. The NAGA heads can disagree among themselves, while Mortal often backs Nishiki or chooses a third line in this review set. That is useful: it forces you to separate blunders from style trade-offs and real insights. Copy the move only when you can state the purchase in points, safety, speed, pressure, or placement.
point-12.whyNot: It is tempting to worship the highest engine line because it feels objective. It is equally tempting to worship LuckyJ because the project is about LuckyJ. Both shortcuts are lazy; neither teaches you why a -3900 risk might be unacceptable in one hand and why a +2900 purchase might be worth preserving in another.
point-12.copy: For every split, write three short claims before looking at the result: what LuckyJ bought, what the engine bought, and what each line risked. If LuckyJ's purchase is clear and reproducible, test it against score, danger, and hand value, then add it to your playbook. If you cannot explain it, file it as uncertain instead of imitating it.
point-12.limit: Do not use engine disagreement to excuse fundamentals. Missed yaku, bad furiten, obvious betaori spots, and no-ten late pushes remain mistakes even if one model split makes them look sophisticated.

point-13.caption: Price the Missing Yakuhai
point-13.situation: An opponent has opened, but their yaku is not yet visible. Their exposed tiles could still be tanyao, honitsu, yakuhai, chanta, or simple atozuke. You hold a loose dragon, the round wind, or that opponent's seat wind, and your own hand is not ready to punish them immediately.
point-13.read: The live yakuhai may be the opponent's missing permission to win, so both carrying it and discarding it have a price. Discarding offers the pon; it is not denial. The deliberate early line releases the tile while no yaku or clear advancement is visible, accepting today's pon risk so the tile is not carried into a more dangerous visible context. The later line chokes it once calls, turn, or river make advancement plausible. Observed cut medians are descriptive because the sample conditions on the tile surviving until each open-hand context; they do not prove that an opponent call caused LuckyJ to wait or reveal the concealed hand's distance.
point-13.whyNot: Keeping the honor preserves the ability to choke the open hand, but it can also become a dangerous live tile that blocks your own route. Releasing it preserves shape but may give the opponent an immediate yaku. Price those two costs directly instead of calling either action automatic defense.
point-13.copy: After every unclear call, mark dragons, round wind, and that player's seat wind as possible yaku switches. Release a singleton only while no yaku or clear advancement is visible; once advancement is visible, choke it unless your own value, safety, or placement makes feeding acceptable.
point-13.limit: The selected examples are engine-contested. Treat the move as a stress test, not a default, and keep the tile when it is your pair, your yaku, your only safe tile, or part of a concrete value plan.

point-14.caption: Safety Has a Target
point-14.situation: You are choosing between trimming shape and spending a tile that is genbutsu, suji, or otherwise safer to one opponent. There is a real or credible threat on the table: riichi, dealer pressure, a fast open hand, or a river that can soon force betaori. The question is whether the defensive tile answers that exact player.
point-14.read: Genbutsu is strongest because it is a same-tile answer to one opponent's river. Suji is weaker but still practical when it points at the player you may need to fold against. LuckyJ's strong results fit this habit: about 13,000 hands, a 22.9% win rate, and only a 10.1% deal-in rate. The placement split is even clearer, with 0.75 deal-ins in top-half games against 1.48 in bottom-half games. The lesson is not to keep every safe-looking tile; it is to keep the one that turns a future forced live discard into a controlled fold or mawashi turn. A tile that can avoid a -4000 loss is worth more than a small amount of shape.
point-14.whyNot: Efficiency hates keeping defensive clutter because the table may stay quiet. That objection is right when the tile has no opponent attached. It is wrong when spending the tile leaves your next bad draw with no answer to the dealer, the riichi player, or the open hand already applying pressure.
point-14.copy: Name the player first, then name the event: riichi, second call, bad draw, or late keiten fight. If the tile is genbutsu or solid suji to that player and your hand is not strong enough to ignore danger, keep it over a marginal shape tile. Recheck the label whenever the main threat changes.
point-14.limit: Do not overrate generic safety. Weak suji, old outside tiles, and genbutsu to a quiet opponent should not block a good hand unless they also defend against the player likely to attack next.

point-15.caption: Stale Safety Costs Shape
point-15.situation: You hold a tile that was safe to someone earlier, but the table has moved on. Another opponent has riichi, the open hand is now the pressure, or your own hand has become close enough that the old safe tile blocks the clean tenpai line. NAGA may prefer preserving the comfort tile while LuckyJ spends it.
point-15.read: Safe tiles have expiration dates. The previous chapter tells you to keep safety for a specific opponent; this chapter tells you to fire it when that opponent is no longer the problem. LuckyJ's over 4,000 stale-safety spends were not reckless attacks, because they were paired with a current-danger check. The same data also supports over 8,400 threat-specific keeps, so the rule is balanced: keep live safety, spend dead safety. A +2300 hand is a real purchase, and letting it decay into a -1500 draw because you protected against the wrong player is not careful mahjong. Careful mahjong is knowing which safety still has value.
point-15.whyNot: The opposing line feels disciplined because it keeps a safe-looking tile in the hand. That feeling is often just fear with a label. If the tile does not answer the live riichi or the player most likely to win, preserving it may only damage your shape and make your next good draw unusable.
point-15.copy: First identify the current danger, then compare your safe tiles against that player. If the old tile protects a quiet opponent, you have another real safe tile, and the hand is close enough to care about shape, discard the stale tile. If those conditions are not met, keep the brake.
point-15.limit: Do not spend stale-looking safety in thin late hands with no second safe tile. Also do not spend it when the original opponent is still the main threat or when betaori is already the best result.

point-16.caption: Attack Through Edges
point-16.situation: The hand is usually middle or late, close enough that preserving tenpai shape matters, and the table has enough danger that a lower-friction discard has value. The choice is between an outside tile—often [[1m]], [[9p]], or a side tile—and a middle tile that keeps the hand connected. You must decide whether the outside cut is merely safe-looking or actually protects the winning shape.
point-16.read: A terminal discard can be an attacking discard when it buys the right to keep the center. Middle tiles connect three-away shapes: [[3p]][[4p]] wants [[2p]] or [[5p]], [[6p]][[7p]] wants [[5p]] or [[8p]], and the tile between them often keeps both possibilities alive. If the outside tile does not support value, yaku, pair structure, or real safety, it may be weaker than it looks. This is why LuckyJ often spends the edge while preserving the inner line. The hand is not giving up; it is choosing the discard that keeps the best win path with the least immediate exposure.
point-16.whyNot: The opposing line is tempting because terminals feel safe and middle tiles feel dangerous. That shortcut misses shape. If the middle tile is the bridge to good tenpai, cutting it can turn a real hand into a decorative collection of safer leftovers.
point-16.copy: When an outside cut looks strange, inspect the tile you keep. If the kept middle tile forms ryanmen, repairs a bad block, preserves perfect one-shanten, or avoids a worse live discard next turn, the edge cut is often the practical attack.
point-16.limit: Do not apply this when the outside tile has a stronger job than the center. Dora terminals, chiitoi pairs, honitsu or chanta material, and exact genbutsu against the main threat must be priced before you call the middle tile essential.

point-18.caption: Label the Honor
point-18.situation: Your hand contains one or more honors while the table is still changing. Some may be your own yakuhai, some may be useful to an open opponent, and some may simply be defensive material. A pure efficiency discard and an honor discard both look plausible.
point-18.read: Start by assigning the honor a role, because different roles create opposite discards. Self-value honors are kept when they create yaku, pair value, honitsu, chiitoi, or dora scaling. Opponent-condition honors are cleaned early when an unclear open hand could use them as its legal yaku. Dead honors and genbutsu honors are defensive currency, but only against the threats they actually answer. The turn split in LuckyJ's data captures this: some lone yakuhai disappear around turn 3, while similar-looking honors in open-hand contexts can wait until around turn 9. Strong honor play is not yakuhai-first or yakuhai-last; it is role-first.
point-18.whyNot: The easy habit is to memorize one slogan: cut honors early, keep honors for safety, or hold yakuhai pairs forever. Each slogan wins some hands and ruins others. Without the role label, you cannot tell whether the tile is earning value for you, feeding legality to someone else, or buying a future fold.
point-18.copy: For each honor, ask four questions in order: is it my yaku or value, is it someone else's missing yaku, is it dead, and is it safe to the real threat? If one answer is clearly strongest, play that role. If two roles conflict, use score and distance: a slow hand behind values self yaku more, while a lead against riichi values defense more.
point-18.limit: Do not keep labeling by habit. Re-check after every call, riichi, second visible copy, and late abnormal river; honors change status faster than suit tiles because one pon can change both legality and danger.
